ThinkMap · Decision Tools

Think it through.

Some of life's most important choices begin with an uncertain question: which degree, which business, which sport, which exam, or how clearly you understand yourself. ThinkMap is a set of free, honest tools for thinking those moments through. Each one makes hidden trade-offs or patterns visible, without taking the decision out of your hands.

No agenda in the output. All agency in the decision.

Education ROI

Is a degree, a coaching year, or a costly course actually worth it?

Weighs the full cost of an education path — fees, years, and the earnings you give up — against what it realistically returns, across dream, base and worst-case scenarios.

Open the calculator How to use

Margin

Should I start this business, or take the steady salary?

Models a business or self-employment path — capital, costs, growth, and the honest chance it fails — against the job you'd otherwise hold, side by side.

Open the calculator How to use

Podium

Is a serious sporting career worth the fifteen-year bet?

Maps an athlete's odds gate by gate, prices prize money, salary and fame as three separate streams, and weighs the whole picture against the ordinary path.

IndiaGlobal How to use

Exam Compass

Which exams actually fit the subjects I'm strong in?

Rate your strengths and it ranks the exams you're best positioned to clear — then tells you what each one truly takes, because the same subjects can be a completely different fight.

IndiaWorld How to use

Mind Mirror

How do I see my own mind - and how well do I know it?

Reflect across eighteen facets of thinking and see the shape of your self-image. It is not an intelligence test - it is a private mirror, with an honest check on how confidently you know yourself.

Open the mirror How to use
✓ Free to use✓ Nothing saved, nothing tracked✓ Works on any phone, no login

Every figure or reflection here is an illustrative starting point, not a forecast, diagnosis, promise, or financial, career, admissions, or psychological advice. These tools exist to help you think, not to tell you what to do.
